summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity makes 5 a quadratic residue modulo such a prime \(p\); choosing an even root \(r\) and setting \(n=r-1\) gives the continued-fraction numerator \(P_2=(n+1)^2-5=pM\), with \(M\le n-1<p\). A telescoping divisibility identity for the numerator recurrence, \(P_2\mid 4(n-1)!-2(n-2)P_3\), shows that \(M\mid P_3\) but \(p\nmid P_3\), so reducing \(P_2/P_3\) cancels exactly the cofactor \(M\) and leaves numerator—and hence the required denominator—equal to \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k= k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}\qquad(2\le k<n-1),
\]
with terminal value
\[
R_{n-1}=(n-1)-\frac{n}{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is \(1/R_2\). We will encode the numerators and denominators of all the \(R_k\)'s by an integer recurrence.

For a fixed \(n\ge 3\), define integers \(P_k\) by
\[
P_n=4,\qquad P_{n-1}=5n-4,
\]
and, for \(2\le k<n-1\),
\[
P_k=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}. \tag{1}
\]
We first record several facts about this recurrence.

### 1. The value and positivity of \(P_2\)

For every \(2\le k\le n-1\), one has the telescoping identity
\[
P_2=(k-1)P_k-k(k-2)P_{k+1}. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, for \(k=2\) this is simply \(P_2=P_2\). If it holds for \(k\), substitute (1):
\[
P_k=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_2
&=(k-1)\bigl(kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}\bigr)-k(k-2)P_{k+1}\\
&=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)(k-1)P_{k+2},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is exactly (2) with \(k\) replaced by \(k+1\).

Taking \(k=n-1\) in (2), and using \(P_{n-1}=5n-4\) and \(P_n=4\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_2
&=(n-2)(5n-4)-4(n-1)(n-3)\\
&=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

We will also need positivity. For \(3\le k\le n-1\), the following stronger downward-induction invariant holds:
\[
P_{k+1}>0,
\qquad
(k-2)P_{k+1}\le P_k. \tag{4}
\]
At \(k=n-1\), this says that \(P_n=4>0\) and
\[
(n-3)4\le 5n-4=P_{n-1},
\]
which is immediate for \(n\ge3\). Now suppose the assertion at \(k+1\) is known. Thus
\[
P_{k+2}>0,\qquad (k-1)P_{k+2}\le P_{k+1}.
\]
Since \(k\ge3\), this first implies \(P_{k+1}>0\). Moreover, by (1),
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_k-(k-2)P_{k+1}
&=2P_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}\\
&\ge \bigl(2(k-1)-(k+1)\bigr)P_{k+2}\\
&=(k-3)P_{k+2}\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (4). It follows that every \(P_k\), \(3\le k\le n\), is positive. Formula (3) shows that \(P_2=(n+1)^2-5>0\) as well.

### 2. Relation to the continued fraction

We claim that
\[
R_k=\frac{P_k}{P_{k+1}}\qquad(2\le k\le n-1). \tag{5}
\]
At the terminal index,
\[
R_{n-1}=(n-1)+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4}=\frac{P_{n-1}}{P_n}.
\]
If (5) holds at \(k+1\), then, using positivity to ensure that the relevant denominator is nonzero,
\[
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}
=k-(k+1)\frac{P_{k+2}}{P_{k+1}}
=\frac{kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}}{P_{k+1}}
=\frac{P_k}{P_{k+1}}.
\]
Thus in particular
\[
R_2=\frac{P_2}{P_3}. \tag{6}
\]
Since the sequence term is the denominator of \(1/R_2\) after reduction, it is the absolute value of the reduced numerator of \(R_2\).

### 3. A divisibility identity

Define, for \(k\ge2\),
\[
G_k=(k-1)!P_k-2(k-2)P_3.
\]
A direct use of recurrence (1), together with the factorial identities
\((k+1)!=(k+1)k!\) and \(k!=k(k-1)!\), gives
\[
G_{k+2}=k(G_{k+1}-G_k) \qquad (2\le k<n-1). \tag{7}
\]
Also
\[
G_2=P_2,
\qquad
G_3=2!P_3-2P_3=0.
\]
It follows inductively from (7) that \(P_2\mid G_k\) for every \(2\le k\le n\). In particular, at \(k=n\), using \(P_n=4\), we obtain the crucial identity
\[
P_2\mid 4(n-1)!-2(n-2)P_3. \tag{8}
\]

### 4. Choosing the index from a square root of 5

Let \(p\) be a prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\). Then \(p\) is odd, \(p\ge7\), and
\[
p\equiv1\quad\hbox{or}\quad4\pmod5. \tag{9}
\]
We claim that \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). Indeed, the nonzero squares modulo \(5\) are \(1\) and \(4\), so (9) says that \(p\) is a square modulo \(5\). Quadratic reciprocity applies to the two odd primes \(5\) and \(p\), and because \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), its sign is positive. Consequently
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
Thus there exists a residue whose square is \(5\) modulo \(p\).

Choose its representative \(a\) with \(0\le a<p\). Of the two roots \(a\) and \(p-a\), exactly one is even, because \(p\) is odd. More explicitly, put
\[
r=\begin{cases}
a,&a\text{ even},\\p-a,&a\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
r\text{ is even},\qquad 0\le r<p,
\qquad p\mid r^2-5. \tag{10}
\]
The even integer \(r\) cannot be \(0\): otherwise \(p\mid5\), impossible since \(p\ge7\). Nor can it be \(2\), because then \(p\mid 2^2-5=-1\). Hence
\[
4\le r<p. \tag{11}
\]

Set
\[
n=r-1.
\]
Then \(n\ge3\), \(n\) is odd, and \(n<p\). By (3),
\[
P_2=(n+1)^2-5=r^2-5.
\]
Therefore \(p\mid P_2\). Since \(P_2>0\), write
\[
P_2=pM \tag{12}
\]
with a positive integer \(M\).

We next show that this cofactor is small. Since \(r=n+1<p\), we have \(p\ge n+1\). If \(M\ge n+1\), then (12) would give
\[
P_2=pM\ge(n+1)^2,
\]
contrary to \(P_2=(n+1)^2-5\). Hence
\[
M<n+1,
\quad\text{so}\quad M\le n. \tag{13}
\]
In fact \(M\ne n\). If \(M=n\), then
\[
pn=n^2+2n-4,
\]
so
\[
4=n(n+2-p).
\]
Thus \(n\mid4\). Since \(n\ge3\) and \(n\) is odd, this forces \(n=3\), but then the displayed equation \(pn=n^2+2n-4\) becomes \(3p=11\), impossible. Therefore
\[
1\le M\le n-1. \tag{14}
\]
It follows that
\[
M\mid(n-1)!. \tag{15}
\]

### 5. Determining exactly what cancels

We first prove that \(p\nmid P_3\). Suppose otherwise. Since \(p\mid P_2\), divisibility identity (8) would imply that \(p\) divides
\[
4(n-1)!-2(n-2)P_3.
\]
The assumed divisibility \(p\mid P_3\) would then force
\[
p\mid4(n-1)!.
\]
As \(p\ge7\), the prime \(p\) does not divide \(4\), and hence it would divide \((n-1)!\). A prime dividing \((n-1)!\) is at most \(n-1\), contradicting \(n<p\). Thus
\[
p\nmid P_3. \tag{16}
\]

We next prove that the entire cofactor \(M\) does divide \(P_3\). Since \(M\mid P_2\), (8) gives
\[
M\mid 4(n-1)!-2(n-2)P_3.
\]
By (15), \(M\mid4(n-1)!\). Subtracting, we obtain
\[
M\mid2(n-2)P_3. \tag{17}
\]
To cancel the first factor in (17), we establish
\[
\gcd(M,2(n-2))=1. \tag{18}
\]

Because \(n\) is odd, \(n+1\) is even, and hence
\[
P_2=(n+1)^2-5
\]
is odd. Thus \(P_2\) is coprime to \(2\). Also, rewriting (3),
\[
P_2=n^2+2n-4=4+(n-2)(n+4). \tag{19}
\]
Any common divisor of \(P_2\) and \(n-2\) therefore divides \(4\). But \(n-2\) is odd, so such a common divisor must be \(1\). Hence \(P_2\) is coprime to both \(2\) and \(n-2\), and therefore to \(2(n-2)\). Since \(M\mid P_2\), the same is true of \(M\), proving (18).

Euclid's lemma applied to (17) and (18) now yields
\[
M\mid P_3. \tag{20}
\]
Write
\[
P_3=Mq. \tag{21}
\]
Here \(q\) is a positive integer, because both \(P_3\) and \(M\) are positive.

Combining (6), (12), and (21), we find
\[
R_2=\frac{P_2}{P_3}=\frac{pM}{Mq}=\frac pq. \tag{22}
\]
Moreover, \(p\) and \(q\) are coprime. Indeed, if the prime \(p\) divided \(q\), then (21) would imply \(p\mid P_3\), contradicting (16).

Thus \(p/q\) in (22) is already in lowest terms, with positive numerator and denominator. Consequently
\[
\frac1{R_2}=\frac qp

after reduction, and its denominator is exactly \(p\). By the definition of A363347, this says
\[
a(n)=p
\]
for the index \(n=r-1\ge3\) constructed above. Therefore every prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs in A363347.
